title: ApplyLocksToAllVehicles on an open model (t6)
verdict: API difference by design, not a parity break
analysis: The spike calls it before CloseModelWithParameters to show it is refused. Python returns False and OR-Tools logs "The model is not closed yet"; ortools-node throws "applyLocksToAllVehicles() needs a closed model" instead of returning a value that is easy to ignore. The port catches that error and records false, so both report apply_locks_before_close=false; the locked and free solves after closing match exactly.

title: Transit callbacks (t2a "python-callback", t2f callback=True)
analysis: Python calls back into the interpreter for every arc evaluation during the search, holding the GIL. ortools-node's registerTransitCallback() evaluates the JS function once per index pair when it is registered and solves on the libuv threadpool without calling JS again, so the search never blocks the event loop. The exact-flavour signatures are identical to the matrix variant in both runtimes.

title: GUIDED_LOCAL_SEARCH with only a solution limit (exact flavour)
verdict: OR-Tools behaviour in both runtimes, not a binding issue
analysis: On about 1 in 10 single-bus instances GLS runs out of new solutions before reaching its solution limit and never stops; Python and Node hang on the same cases (first seen on t2a case 3 at solution_limit=10). The exact flavour therefore adds a guard time limit far above the normal solve time. Guarded cases are listed in the parity table, still compared (they matched), and left out of the latency tables.

title: SetAllowedVehiclesForIndex on Python 9.15 (google/or-tools#5415)
verdict: Python binding bug, absent in ortools-node
analysis: Python 9.15.6755 raises TypeError (absl::Span argument) for SetAllowedVehiclesForIndex, so the spike falls back to removing the other vehicles from VehicleVar. ortools-node accepts setAllowedVehiclesForIndex() on both pins. Parity is checked in the mode Python uses on each pin (span on 9.14, removevalues on 9.15); the latency appendix times both modes in Node.

title: Routing solve latency vs Python on OR-Tools 9.15 (t2b, 20 buses, GLS sl=50)
verdict: Mostly glibc malloc's single-thread fast path (~19%); ~3% the binding's interrupt/onSolution hooks; ~4% the libortools build
analysis: Baseline: OR-Tools 9.15, Python 3.13 single-threaded vs Node async, pinned to CPU 0, 5 repeats x 60 cases (300 solves each), one idle machine; every ratio below is per case against that baseline. Solve p50 1482 ms in Python, 1880 ms in Node async, 1975 ms in Node sync: Node/Python 1.28 (p10 1.24, p90 1.30). Both find identical solutions with identical branches, failures and solutions counts, so they do the same work; build (2.56 vs 3.49 ms) and read (0.09 vs 0.49 ms) are faster in Node, and sync vs async is not a factor. (1) glibc malloc takes a lock-free fast path only while a process has one thread; the Python baseline has one, a Node process never does. One idle thread in Python makes its solve 1.19x slower, leaving Node 1.07x behind; GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=1000 cuts Node solve p50 to 1304 ms, within 1.05x of Python with the same setting. (2) The binding adds a custom search limit (interrupt()) and an at-solution hook (onSolution) to every RoutingModel; the same two in Python cost it about 3% (1443 to 1494 ms). (3) Loading the Python wheel's libortools into Node (LD_LIBRARY_PATH) moves the ratio from 1.28 to 1.235, so about 4% is the C++ archive build. The tunable is read only at process start, so the binding cannot set it; there is no cheap binding fix. The 9.14 gap (0.79x in the latency table) was not analysed. Scripts and per-case results: bench/dispatch/experiments/t2b/.

title: Not investigated: Node slower on many tiny solves
verdict: Open; likely a fixed per-solve overhead
analysis: Workloads made of many solves of a few milliseconds or less are slower in Node: t2d two-stage 600 single-bus solves 0.52x (9.14) / 0.61x (9.15), t1 solve 0.43x (9.14), set cover 0.61x and math_opt knapsack MIP 0.62x (9.15) in the latency tables. The results are identical; the cost per call (parameter conversion, the threadpool hop, the hooks above, malloc) was not measured.

verdict: Time limit, not a model difference
analysis: On 2 of 300 cold PATH_CHEAPEST_ARC cases the first solution takes about the whole 1 s limit: Python stopped at 1001 ms with ROUTING_FAIL_TIMEOUT, Node found its first solution at 885 ms and 959 ms. On 9.15 every case agrees, and the exact-flavour t2a workloads are identical on both pins.

verdict: Time limit (300 ms GLS), not a model difference
analysis: Of the 300 ms GLS solves, 5 (9.14) and 4 (9.15) end in different local optima: on 9.14 Node is better in all 5 (e.g. stay:off/12: one more newcomer served, 40,007,313 vs 60,006,509), on 9.15 worse in all 4 (e.g. gender:on/58 and gender:off/58: one newcomer fewer, 20,006,921 vs 7,130). The exact-flavour t2c workloads (same model, solution limit instead of a time limit) are identical, 320/320 on both pins. That Node lands worse on 9.15 fits its slower search per iteration (see the t2b latency finding) but was not measured separately.

verdict: Time-limited difference: Node serves one newcomer fewer on both pins
analysis: The 200-bus model under a 3000 ms GLS limit: objective Python 820,521,086 vs Node 840,518,994 on 9.14 and Python 840,518,994 vs Node 860,517,702 on 9.15, both ROUTING_PARTIAL_SUCCESS_LOCAL_OPTIMUM_NOT_REACHED. Each gap is about 2 x BIG_PENALTY (10,000,000 per unserved pickup and per unserved delivery), so Node leaves one more newcomer unassigned. The same model with a solution limit (exact flavour, t2d 200 buses sl=30) is identical in both runtimes, so this is search progress within the time limit, consistent with Node's slower search per iteration (t2b finding); a dispatcher on Node needs a somewhat longer limit for the same result.

verdict: Expected: the spike measures that time-limited solves are not reproducible
analysis: The loaded time-limited runs vary between 960,508,411 and 1,000,504,178 within each runtime (Python itself returns both values across its 6 loaded runs); Node 9.15 once returns 980,506,300. The solution-limited half (sl/*) returns 440,556,967 in all 16 runs of every runtime and pin.
